title: In Psalms 57 How Can We Cultivate A Heart Of Praise Even When Facing Adversity
paragraphs: Cultivating a Heart of Praise in Adversity: Lessons from Psalm 57

Psalm 57 is a remarkable example of worship in the midst of danger and uncertainty. Written by David "when he fled from Saul, in the cave," this psalm is both a desperate plea for mercy and a declaration of steadfast praise. By examining David’s response to adversity, believers today can learn how to cultivate a heart of praise even in their darkest moments.
The Context: Worship in the Cave
David was being pursued by King Saul, forced to hide in a cave to escape certain death. In this vulnerable and frightening moment, David’s first words are a cry for mercy:
Be merciful unto me, O God, be merciful unto me; For my soul taketh refuge in thee: Yea, in the shadow of thy wings will I take refuge, Until these calamities be overpast. - Psalm 57:1 ASV
David’s posture is not one of self-reliance but of humble dependence on God. Even in adversity, he acknowledges God's sovereignty and protection.
Turning to God in Prayer and Praise
David’s response to fear is not bitterness or complaint, but prayerful trust. He seeks God’s help and expresses confidence in God’s faithfulness:
I will cry unto God Most High, Unto God that performeth all things for me. - Psalm 57:2 ASV
Even as he faces enemies, David sets his heart to praise:
My heart is fixed, O God, my heart is fixed: I will sing, yea, I will sing praises. - Psalm 57:7 ASV
This steadfastness reveals a deliberate choice—David chooses to praise God, regardless of his circumstances.
How Can We Develop This Kind of Heart?
Seek Refuge in God, Not in Circumstances
David’s security is not in the cave, but “in the shadow of thy wings.” Our hearts are anchored by trusting in God’s character and promises, not by our ability to control our situation.
Remember God’s Faithfulness
David recalls God’s acts of deliverance and faithfulness. Meditating on Scripture and remembering personal testimonies of God’s goodness strengthen our resolve to praise.
For thy lovingkindness is great unto the heavens, And thy truth unto the skies. - Psalm 57:10 ASV
Choose Praise as an Act of the Will
David says, “I will sing, yea, I will sing praises.” Praise is not always spontaneous in adversity; often, it is a choice rooted in faith.
Awake up, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake right early. - Psalm 57:8 ASV
Desire God’s Glory Above All
Even in trouble, David’s concern is that God be exalted:
Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens; Let thy glory be above all the earth. - Psalm 57:5 ASV
The ultimate aim of praise is to lift up God’s name, not simply to change our feelings or circumstances.
New Testament Insights: Praise in the Face of Trouble

The New Testament echoes this theme. Paul and Silas, imprisoned and beaten, prayed and sang hymns to God (Acts 16:25 ASV). Believers are exhorted to “rejoice in the Lord always” (Philippians 4:4 ASV), because our joy and praise are rooted in Christ, not in changing circumstances.
Practical Steps for Today
Start and end your day with praise, focusing on God’s attributes and promises.
In times of trouble, intentionally recall and thank God for past faithfulness.
Sing or listen to worship music that proclaims God’s truth.
Pray for a heart that desires God’s glory above your own comfort.
Conclusion

Psalm 57 teaches that praise is not reserved for easy times. In fact, it becomes most powerful in adversity. When we fix our hearts on God—His mercy, faithfulness, and glory—we can cultivate a life of praise, no matter what we face. This is possible because of the ultimate deliverance found in Jesus Christ, who gives us reason to rejoice in every season.
